blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights three papers from the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) domain, focusing on empirical evaluations and architectural innovations. The first paper, 'Return of the devil in the details: delving deep into convolutional nets' by Chatfield et al. (2014), conducts a rigorous comparison between shallow feature encodings (e.g., Improved Fisher Vector) and CNN-based methods for image classification. The study finds that while data augmentation (e.g., flipping and cropping) improves performance for both shallow and deep methods, CNNs still outperform shallow encodings by a significant margin (~10%). Fine-tuning and architectural choices (e.g., CNN-M and CNN-S) further enhance results, with fine-tuning contributing ~2.7% improvement. The second paper, 'Spatial pyramid pooling in deep convolutional networks for visual recognition' by He et al. (2014), addresses the limitation of CNNs requiring fixed-size inputs by introducing a spatial pyramid pooling (SPP) layer. SPP allows CNNs to handle arbitrary image sizes and aspect ratios by dividing feature maps into spatial bins and pooling responses at multiple granularities. The technique improves accuracy across multiple architectures and enables significant speedups (38x-102x) in object detection tasks like R-CNN. The third paper, 'Very deep convolutional networks for large-scale image recognition' by Simonyan & Zisserman (2014), explores the impact of network depth on classification accuracy. Using a fixed setup with 3x3 convolutional filters and ReLU activations, the authors demonstrate that deeper networks (up to 19 layers) achieve lower error rates, though performance saturates beyond this depth. Local response normalization (LRN) is found to be ineffective and adds computational overhead.
paper_title: Return of the devil in the details: delving deep into convolutional nets
paper_abstract: Many deep neural networks trained on natural images exhibit a curious phenomenon in common: on the first layer they learn features similar to Gabor filters and color blobs. Such first-layer features appear not to be specific to a particular dataset or task, but general in that they are applicable to many datasets and tasks. Features must eventually transition from general to specific by the last layer of the network, but this transition has not been studied extensively. In this paper we experimentally quantify the generality versus specificity of neurons in each layer of a deep convolutional neural network and report a few surprising results. Transferability is negatively affected by two distinct issues: (1) the specialization of higher layer neurons to their original task at the expense of performance on the target task, which was expected, and (2) optimization difficulties related to splitting networks between co-adapted neurons, which was not expected. In an example network trained on ImageNet, we demonstrate that either of these two issues may dominate, depending on whether features are transferred from the bottom, middle, or top of the network. We also document that the transferability of features decreases as the distance between the base task and target task increases, but that transferring features even from distant tasks can be better than using random features. A final surprising result is that initializing a network with transferred features from almost any number of layers can produce a boost to generalization that lingers even after fine-tuning to the target dataset.
